item.title: Climate change is projected to widen global inequalities in ocean-derived wellbeing
item.description:
Yaowen Zhang, Qutu Jiang, Xinying Lin, Qiongyao Dai, Conrad A. Pilditch, Cuicui Feng, Jihua Zhang, Mingzhao Hu, et al.
Communications Earth & Environment
DOI: 10.1038/s43247-026-04070-1
Abstract Climate change threatens well-being from the ocean by disrupting both marine and economic systems, yet its global implications remain unclear. Here, we introduce the Blue Well-being Index (BWI) to assess and predict the performance of ocean-derived well-being for 143 coastal countries under climate change scenarios. We find that although the historical assessment reveals an improvement in the global average BWI score from 2000 to 2021, future projections under high-emission climate scenarios (SSP5-8.5) indicate disproportionate losses across 143 countries. In SSP 5-8.5, global BWI is projected to decline by ~9% by 2100, with adverse effects in nearly 90% of coastal countries. Under the climate-mitigation SSP1-2.6 scenario, with projections indicating that the world could achieve an overall ~11% improvement in BWI across 76% of coastal nations. Climate change exacerbates blue well-being losses, disproportionately affecting both low‑income and high‑income countries, particularly in the natural and social dimensions. These findings underscore the importance of coordinated international mitigation and ocean-conservation efforts to safeguard human well-being and ocean health.

item.title: Upscaling sediment source prediction for watershed management
item.description:
Abigal Percich, Allen Gellis, James F. Fox, Admin Husic
Communications Earth & Environment
DOI: 10.1038/s43247-026-04097-4
Abstract Identifying sources of erosion is critical for effective watershed management, but existing fingerprinting methods remain resource-intensive and difficult to standardize or scale. To address this, we compiled a global synthesis of 142 sediment tracing studies across 267 watersheds and developed an explainable machine learning framework that predicts sediment provenance using remotely sensed attributes. Four sediment categories capture global erosion sources—subsurface, cultivated, non-cultivated, and infrastructure—and our model predicts their contributions with robust accuracy (R 2 = 0.40–0.53). Model interpretation confirms that predictions align with expected hydroclimatic and land cover relationships, indicating consistency with the physical processes governing sediment sourcing. When applied to six watersheds in the United States and United Kingdom, the model reveals contrasting erosional regimes: subsurface erosion dominates the Upper Mississippi and Chesapeake Bay, whereas non-cultivated surface erosion prevails across the UK watersheds. This predictive framework provides a transferable, interpretable, and data-driven tool for mapping sediment sources at large scales, enabling targeted watershed management.

item.title: Lake eutrophication increases unprotected organic carbon pools in sediments
item.description:
Youzi Gong, Cai Li, Yue Yang, Xue Jiang, Yang Gu, Jipeng Song, Yan Wang, Musong Chen, et al.
Communications Earth & Environment
DOI: 10.1038/s43247-026-04103-9
Abstract Reactive iron oxide-bound organic carbon (Fe–OC) is a key pathway for long-term carbon burial, but its effectiveness under increasingly widespread eutrophication remains uncertain. Here we show that Fe–OC accounts for 16% of total organic carbon and buries at ~14 Mt C yr −1 in lakes globally, equivalent to ~27% of the marine Fe–OC sink despite lakes covering only ~1.25% of marine area. However, bloom-prone lakes exhibit lower Fe–OC content and contribution to sedimentary organic carbon than non–bloom-prone lakes. Field observations and incubation experiments further reveal that bloom-induced redox fluctuations and low-aromaticity algal organic matter inputs jointly accelerate Fe–OC turnover and reduce organic carbon loading on Fe minerals, causing Fe–OC losses of up to ~68%. These findings suggest that eutrophication weakens the long-term carbon burial capacity of lakes by increasing unprotected organic carbon pools in sediments, necessitating reevaluation of their contributions to the global carbon budget.
